Questions 1–7, 10, 12), Codex Turn 49 (§2–§9, §13.6, §14 and Questions 1–14), Codex Turn 50

Nothing below may be changed after the first cell has executed; a change means a new schedule, a

into `schedule_id` (§3.1 below), so the document must be final before the schedule is sealed and
therefore cannot name the id it is about to produce. The binding runs both ways all the same: the

---

## 1. What is being compared

Three client-side **replay arms**, identical in world, prompt, tool schema and episode ceiling,
differing only in what the client puts on the wire on every turn after the first:

| arm | per-turn completion cap | reasoning replayed | observation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A′** | 8,000 | yes | whole-ledger read |
| **B1′** | 16,000 | yes | whole-ledger read |
| **B2′** | 8,000 | **no** (`reasoning_content` dropped from the wire projection) | whole-ledger read |

The rollout state's own trajectory keeps every model's reasoning under all three arms; only the
projection differs. Dropping a `None`-valued `reasoning_content` is **provider hygiene under every
arm**, not the B2′ intervention (Codex §2).

### The three replay classes (Codex T48b §1)

1. **assistant-visible / semantic content** — text and tool calls. Replayed verbatim in every arm.
2. **hidden reasoning content** — `reasoning_content`. Replaying it *is* the treatment: on in
   A′/B1′, off in B2′.
3. **opaque provider continuation metadata** — signatures/handles a provider emits with a tool call
   that must be replayed verbatim to continue it. **Declared UNSUPPORTED by this client**
   (`measure_budget.UNSUPPORTED_CONTINUATION_FIELDS = ("thought_signature",)`). A provider/model
   family that requires one is `capability_incompatible` — excluded from the whole comparison
   before any cell runs, never counted against an arm and never called a model failure.

---

## 2. Inference population and estimand

**The estimand is the average arm contrast over this exact fixed panel** of
(provider, model, selector) strata — four models × six selectors = 24 strata. Replicate randomness
is nested inside a stratum.

This is **not** an estimate for "models in general" or for "generated bookkeeping tasks in
general". The roster and the selector panel are FIXED factors, not a random sample from any
population, and no sentence in Turn 49 may generalise past the panel. The selector is the sampling
unit *within* the panel; a cluster-by-selector sensitivity analysis is reported alongside the
primary interval and is descriptive only, because six clusters cannot support a narrow one.

Every (provider, model) is analysed **separately**. There is no four-model mixture, no pooled
mean over models, and no declared weighting that would create one.

---

## 3. Roster, panel and design

**Provider: Mistral only.** Gemini was excluded **before randomisation**, on evidence recorded
before any confirmatory cell: a real `gemini-2.5-flash` rollout was rate-limited through all six
of the pacing loop's back-offs (20 s → 120 s) and could not sustain the tool loop on the free
tier. That is an `exogenous` quota exclusion of a whole configuration, decided blind to any arm
outcome, and it is recorded here rather than appearing later as a stream of failed cells.
NVIDIA is excluded for cost (25–28 minutes a cell); Groq (8K tokens/minute per request),
Cerebras (8K context) and OpenRouter (50 requests/day) cannot run a rollout at all.

| factor | levels |
|---|---|
| provider | `mistral` |
| model | `devstral-2512`, `ministral-14b-2512`, `ministral-8b-2512`, `mistral-medium-2508` |
| selector | `train:1`, `train:12`, `train:30`, `eval:5`, `train:3:hard`, `train:107:hard` |
| arm | A′, B1′, B2′ |
| replicate | 1, 2 |

4 × 6 × 3 × 2 = **144 cells**.

**Pins.** temperature 0.0, top-p 1.0, no seed (no reachable endpoint honours one —
`tests/seed_probe.py`; replication is the tool instead), episode output ceiling 40,000 tokens,
framework rollout retries **0**, SDK retries **0** (`ClientConfig(max_retries=0)`; the library
default of 10 lives inside `AsyncOpenAI`, below the wire capture, where a discarded late 200 is
billed and invisible), request timeout 600 s, ≥ 6 s between provider calls.

### Order balance — claimed exactly where it holds

Six selectors is **one complete Williams cycle per (provider, model, replicate)**:

> every arm occupies every position exactly equally often AND every ordered adjacent pair of
> distinct arms occurs exactly equally often, WITHIN each (provider, model, replicate) layer.
> Order balance is claimed at the **(provider, model)** level; it is **NOT** claimed within a
> single selector, where each (provider, model, selector, replicate) block runs exactly one of the
> six sequences.

Per selector (8 blocks, not a multiple of 6) balance is **approximate** and is reported as such.
`tests/arm_table.py` prints the sequence/position/adjacency census at the (provider, model),
selector and (provider, model, selector) levels and labels each stratum exact or approximate —
the schedule's claim is verified against the cells actually dealt, never asserted from the
construction.

### 3.1 Schedule identity: the sealed EXPERIMENT CONTRACT (Codex T49 §2)

The schedule is written once, before any rollout, by `tests/schedule_arms.py --seal`, and
`schedule_id` is the sha256 of its canonical content (everything but `created_at` and the id
itself). `tests/run_arms.py` refuses to execute a file that no longer hashes to its own id.

Version 1 hashed the roster, the selectors, the arm **labels**, the order, the sampling pins and
the ceilings. It did not hash what those labels MEAN. `run_arms.cell_command` passes `--arm A`;
`measure_budget.ARM_PRESETS` supplies `(8000 tokens, replay on)` at execution time — so the
treatment could be edited while `schedule_id` stayed the same. The same held for the world (a
manifest rotation makes `train:1` a different public task under an unchanged selector string), the
code, the installed libraries, the failure map and this document.

A **v2 (sealed, confirmatory)** schedule therefore carries an `experiment_contract` INSIDE the
hashed content:

| field | what it binds | computed from |
|---|---|---|
| `instrument_commit` | the commit whose execution tree was sealed | `git rev-parse HEAD` |
| `execution_paths` | the CLOSED set of paths whose content IS the instrument | `schedule_arms.EXECUTION_PATHS` |
| `execution_excludes` | what the on-disk walk skips inside that set | `schedule_arms.EXECUTION_EXCLUDES` |
| `execution_tree_digest` | the BYTES ON DISK under those paths | sha256 over sorted (relative path, sha256 of the file) |
| `execution_tree_file_count` | how many files that was | the same walk |
| `instrument_identity_version` | the ALGORITHM that computes the tree identity | `schedule_arms.INSTRUMENT_IDENTITY_VERSION` |
| `runtime_environment_digest` | the BYTES of every installed distribution, of every file no RECORD references, and of the interpreter | sha256 over the runtime-environment manifest (§3.1a) |
| `runtime_environment_file_count`, `_bytes`, `_distribution_count`, `_extra_file_count` | how much that was, and how much of it no RECORD claims | the same walk |
| `runtime_environment_identity_version` | the ALGORITHM that computes the environment identity | `schedule_arms.RUNTIME_ENVIRONMENT_IDENTITY_VERSION` |
| `python_version` | the interpreter's own version string, beside its authenticated bytes | `sys.version` |
| `analysis_plan_sha256` | this document, by content | its own bytes |
| `arm_contract` | `A=(8000, replay on)`, `B1=(16000, on)`, `B2=(8000, off)` | the literal `measure_budget.ARM_PRESETS` |
| `expected_episode_contract_digest` | observation and termination rules, at the pinned ceiling | `beancount_ledger.episode_contract_digest(40_000)` |
| `expected_replay_contract_digest_by_arm` | the provider-bound replay policy, per arm | `measure_budget.replay_contract_digest` |
| `package_lock` | `verifiers`, `openai`, the interpreter | `importlib.metadata` |
| `failure_map_digest` | the ordered bucket rules, the quota table and the window-rule constants | sha256 over `arm_table`'s own constants |
| `manifest.rotation_id`, `manifest.manifest_content_digest` | which release manifest is active | `graph.manifest`'s own path/rotation resolution |
| `expected_public_task_id_by_selector` | the WORLD each selector serves | one `load_environment(selector)` per selector |
| `provider_quotas` | the TPM/rps table a 429 is classified against, and its date | `arm_table.MODEL_QUOTAS` |

`schedule_id` now names the treatment, the world, the code and the analysis — not merely the order
in which three mutable labels are invoked. Mutating any one of those fields moves the id
(witnessed in `tests/test_measure_budget.py`).

#### The identity rule: a GIT-PATH CONTRACT, not commit equality (Codex T50 §1)

The v2 witness compared `git rev-parse HEAD` to the sealed `instrument_commit` for **exact
equality**. That rule cannot be satisfied by its own storage workflow. The sealed schedule is a
file in this repository: committing it MOVES HEAD, so the schedule can never be executed from the
commit it names. Codex Turn 50 found precisely that — sealed at `cf613c1…`, HEAD at `5d03346…`,
the diff confined to `DURUM.md`, `GECE.md`, `design_chat/to_codex.md` and the schedule file itself
— and the command shown in Turn 50 would have returned exit 3 at its own startup witness, before
request 1.

Relaxing equality to "ancestor" is **not** the fix either: a descendant commit may change Python.
The security property is the PATH/CONTENT constraint.

**And the content must be read from the DISK, not from git.** The first version of this rule asked
git three questions — `status`, `diff`, `ls-tree` — and an adversarial review defeated all three
without ever turning the witness red, because every one of them answers about the INDEX rather than
about the bytes the interpreter will import:

- `git update-index --assume-unchanged tests/measure_budget.py`, then edit the file. `status` is
  silent, `ls-tree` reports the sealed blob, and the digest recomputed to the sealed value while the
  file on disk had changed. (`--skip-worktree` behaves the same way.)
- **Module shadowing.** `measure_budget.py` inserts the package ROOT at `sys.path[0]` and `tests/`
  right behind it, so ANY new `environments/beancount_ledger/<name>.py` is imported BEFORE the real
  module of that name — and it sat outside all three sealed subtrees. A live attack resolved
  `import openai` to an unsealed `environments/beancount_ledger/openai.py`; `package_lock` cannot
  see it, because `importlib.metadata` reads distribution metadata, not the module that was
  actually imported. `tests/` siblings can shadow the instrument's own modules the same way.
- A new file inside `tests/` hidden by a `.gitignore` line. `.gitignore` lives on an EVIDENCE path,
  so committing the line is permitted, and the file it hides is invisible to both `status` and
  `ls-tree` while `tests/` is `sys.path[0]` of every cell process.

**The digest procedure.** The seal walks the execution root on disk —
`environments/beancount_ledger/` — skipping `reviews/**` (evidence), `.venv/**` (the interpreter's
own installed libraries: gitignored, tens of thousands of files, and already bound by
`package_lock`'s pinned `verifiers`/`openai`/interpreter versions and by the replay-contract
digests), `**/__pycache__/**` and `*.pyc`. It reads every remaining file's ACTUAL BYTES and hashes
the sorted `(relative path, sha256)` pairs together with the root and the exclusion list. **The
relative file SET is part of the digest material**, so an ADDED or REMOVED file moves the digest
even when every surviving file is untouched — which is what catches both shadowing vectors — and
reading the bytes is what catches `--assume-unchanged`. The file COUNT is sealed beside the digest
so an addition is named as an addition rather than surfacing as an opaque hash mismatch. An empty
execution set produces NO digest and the seal refuses: a digest over nothing compares equal to a
digest over nothing. The walk is ~320 files and ~4.6 MB here — about 40 ms warm, a few seconds
cold — once per session start.

The startup witness therefore requires, before request 1:

1. **the on-disk digest** — the recomputed execution-tree digest equals the sealed one (PRIMARY);
2. **the on-disk file count** — equal to the sealed one, and every file readable (PRIMARY);
3. **the sealed path set and exclusion list** — the ones this instrument still declares;
4. **ancestry** — the sealed commit is reachable from the runtime HEAD, or is it (SECONDARY);
5. **an empty execution diff** — `git diff <instrument_commit>..HEAD` is EMPTY over the execution
   paths, and the changed files are NAMED when it is not (SECONDARY);
6. **a clean execution tree** — `git status --porcelain` is empty over those paths (SECONDARY). A
   dirty EVIDENCE file (`reviews/`, `design_chat/`, a root `*.md`) does **not** fail: those files
   are written by the run, and an experiment that cannot write its own log while it runs is not an
   experiment.

The git rows are kept because they say something the walk cannot — which commit this content
corresponds to, and what a reviewer would read as the diff — but they no longer carry the identity
on their own.

Everything outside the execution paths, and everything the exclusion list skips, is EVIDENCE or is
bound elsewhere: the schedule by `schedule_id`, this document by `analysis_plan_sha256`, a
configuration exclusion by its `record_digest`, the installed libraries by `package_lock` and the
replay-contract digests.

**The runtime HEAD is recorded separately** — on every archived row (`runtime_head`,
`execution_tree_digest`, `runtime_environment_digest`, `instrument_identity_version`) and on every
execution-journal entry — because under this contract the executing commit may legitimately differ
from the sealed one, and the report must state both. The table's *Instrument identity* section
prints them side by side; since Codex Turn 51 §2 a row whose digests differ from the seal is
**refused from exact admission and from every estimand**, not marked DIFFERENT and counted anyway.

#### 3.1a The RUNTIME ENVIRONMENT is sealed as BYTES, not as versions (Codex T51 §1)

The execution-tree digest stops at the repository boundary: `.venv/**` is excluded from it. The
replacement binding used to be version STRINGS — `importlib.metadata.version("openai")`,
`version("verifiers")`, `sys.version` — recomputed by the startup witness from the same source
that produced them. Codex Turn 51 §1: an in-place edit to a file under
`.venv/Lib/site-packages/openai/` changes request construction, retries, response interpretation
or token accounting while `METADATA` still reports the sealed version. It passes the
execution-tree digest, the package lock and the replay-contract digests. It is the site-packages
analogue of the module-shadow attack, it needs no new distribution and no `sys.path` change, and
the transitive packages were even less covered than the two named ones.

**What is walked.** `schedule_arms.runtime_environment_manifest()`:

1. **every file under every directory the running interpreter can import from** — the site-package
   roots AND the STANDARD LIBRARY — hashed from its actual bytes. Not only the two named
   distributions, not only the files a RECORD happens to mention, and not only what pip installed:
   hashing `python312.dll` does not cover `json/encoder.py`, `ssl.py`, `subprocess.py` or
   `asyncio/`, and those shape every provider request. Nested roots are dropped, so the venv's own
   `Lib` (which contains `site-packages`) is walked once, not twice;
2. **every installed distribution's `RECORD`**, enumerated: each referenced entry is located, its
   RECORD-DECLARED sha256 is verified against the bytes on disk wherever the wheel published one,
   a mismatch is recorded per distribution, a referenced file that no longer exists is recorded as
   missing, and an entry that resolves OUTSIDE the roots (a console script in `Scripts/`, a data
   file) is located through the distribution and hashed there. `*.dist-info/RECORD` is itself
   hashed as bytes;
3. **the files under site-packages that NO RECORD references** — the shadow analogue: an added
   module is invisible to `importlib.metadata` exactly as a shadowing `.py` beside the package was
   invisible to `package_lock`;
4. **the interpreter, as bytes** — `sys.executable` itself plus the `pythonXY` runtime library
   beside it, falling back to `sys.base_prefix` when the venv's `Scripts/` carries only the
   launcher (which is the case here) — plus `sys.version`;
5. **the IMPORT ENVIRONMENT itself** (identity version 2, C1 of the adversarial review of these
   closures). `PYTHONPATH` is not a file under any root: a directory named there is PREPENDED to
   `sys.path` and shadows any sealed module — `openai/`, `json/`, `ssl.py` — while every hashed
   byte, and therefore the whole digest, stays identical. `sys_path_survey()` classifies every
   `sys.path` entry as `walked` (inside a hashed root), `execution_tree` (inside the package
   directory, sealed by the OTHER half of the instrument identity), `file` (a `pythonXY.zip`,
   hashed), `absent` (a slot with nothing at it — sealed as absent BECAUSE creating
   `base_prefix/python312.zip` would shadow the entire standard library) or **`uncovered`**.
   Uncovered entries are walked too, so their bytes reach the digest, and are reported as an
   explicit sealed list; `[]` is the healthy state and is what this machine reports. The startup
   witness has its own row for that list, so an injection live at startup is NAMED rather than
   surfacing as an opaque digest mismatch, and the sealer refuses to seal a contaminated one;
6. **the rest of `sys.path`** (C3). Four real members were outside the walk: `base_prefix/DLLs`
   (37 extension modules — `_ssl.pyd`, `_socket.pyd`, `select.pyd`, `pyexpat.pyd`, every one of
   them on the path of a provider request and none of them a `.py` under `Lib`), the
   `base_prefix/pythonXY.zip` slot, `prefix/pyvenv.cfg` (which names the interpreter this venv
   points at and whether the system site-packages are visible), and every file in `Scripts/` that
   no RECORD references (an added `python.bat` shim, a replaced `activate`). The roots are now
   taken from `sys.path` itself, keeping the entries inside `sys.prefix`/`sys.base_prefix` — which
   on this machine collapses to those two prefixes and subsumes all four in two walks.

Two records found twice are ONE record. `importlib.metadata` enumerates per `sys.path` entry, so a
root present on `sys.path` twice reports all 112 distributions twice and would move the digest with
nothing on disk having changed; identical records (identical down to the `base_key` that says where
the distribution was found) are collapsed, and a genuinely shadowing second copy — a different
directory, hence a different key — stays visible as the two distributions it is.

The per-distribution RECORD verdicts (`missing`, `declared_hash_mismatch`, `record_entries`) are
part of the hashed material, not commentary: a distribution whose declared hash stops matching is a
changed environment even if some other file's bytes moved to compensate. An environment that
yields NO file produces NO digest and the seal refuses — a digest over nothing compares equal to a
digest over nothing.

**The roots come from the RUNNING INTERPRETER** (`sysconfig` → `sys.prefix`), never from a path
relative to this checkout. A builder worktree has no `.venv` at all, and the digest must describe
the interpreter that will execute cells. Keys are stated relative to `sys.prefix` /
`sys.base_prefix` (`prefix/Lib/site-packages/openai/_client.py`, `base_prefix/python312.dll`) so
the manifest reads as a description of that environment rather than of one machine's directory
layout.

**Bytecode is excluded by name, and the exclusion is SOUND rather than merely convenient.**
`__pycache__/` directories and `*.pyc` are skipped: bytecode is written by the very act of
importing, so a strict `.pyc` set would not be stationary across the run it is supposed to
authenticate — and this venv is shared by every process on the machine, so a third party's import
would turn the digest red mid-experiment.

An earlier draft called an in-place `.pyc` edit insufficient "because any regeneration comes from
sealed bytes". That was wrong, and C2 of the adversarial review demonstrated it end-to-end: an
EXISTING cache file edited in place keeps the source mtime and size recorded in its own 16-byte
header, so the default timestamp validation accepts it forever, the tampered body executes, and the
sealed `.py` is never read — no regeneration ever happens. What makes the exclusion sound is that
**no pre-existing cache is on the path at all**. `run_arms` points `PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX` (and its
in-process twin `sys.pycache_prefix`) at a FRESH per-session directory under the OS temp — for its
own process, before it imports the package, and for every cell subprocess, which therefore has it
from process start. The fresh tree is empty, so every module is compiled from the `.py` bytes this
manifest hashed, and the only `.pyc` the exclusion skips are ones this session generated from those
bytes. The prefix is journalled (`cell_environment_sealed`), so a reader can see which tree a
session used.

**The exclusion set, completely.** (i) `__pycache__/` and `*.pyc`, sound as above. (ii) The
EXECUTION TREE: the package directory is on `sys.path` and is deliberately not hashed here — it has
its own digest, and `reviews/**` inside it is evidence written BY the run, so folding it in would
make the environment digest move every time a row is archived. (iii) Anything outside `sys.path`
and outside both prefixes: the OS, the C runtime, DLLs an extension module resolves through `PATH`,
and any file no `RECORD` names. (iv) An uncovered `sys.path` directory that CONTAINS a walked root
or the execution root is named but not walked — `PYTHONPATH=C:\` would otherwise be an hour-long
walk, and the refusal does not depend on having hashed it. (v) A file that cannot be read is
recorded under `unreadable`, which is part of the digest material, rather than hashed. (vi) The
ORDER of `sys.path` is reported (`sys_path_order`) but not sealed: the sealer, the executor and
each cell build it by the same insertions in a different sequence, and order matters only between
two entries that are both hashed, or against an entry that is `uncovered` and therefore refused
whatever its position. (vii) Environment variables other than the three import-injecting ones
(`PYTHONPATH`, `PYTHONHOME`, `PYTHONSTARTUP`) are not sealed.

**Measured on this machine** (2026-08-31, the real venv and the real interpreter, identity version
2): **19,178 files, 432,376,226 bytes**, 112 distributions, 1,211 standard-library files, **2 files
referenced by no RECORD** (`virtualenv`'s own `_virtualenv.pth` / `_virtualenv.py` — the whole
no-RECORD signal, not drowned by the stdlib, which is counted separately), **0 uncovered `sys.path`
entries**, 0 unreadable, 0 RECORD-declared hash mismatches. C3 added 1,571 files and 27.6 MB over
identity version 1's 17,607 / 404,763,035 — `DLLs/` (37 files, 17.9 MB), all of `Scripts/`
(59 files, 2.3 MB), `pyvenv.cfg`, and the rest of the two prefixes (`include/`, `libs/`, `tcl/`).
Cost, honestly as a range rather than one number: **≈3–5 s** with the environment fully in the page
cache, **≈15–25 s** when it is partly evicted (the ordinary case between cells), and **≈460 s** on
the first cold read, when Windows Defender scans every file for the first time — measured, and up
from ≈400–450 s at version 1. `hashlib.file_digest` streams each file rather than materialising it,
which is what keeps 432 MB a seconds-scale operation at all. The per-CELL verification schedule
below is unchanged by this: the walk is still seconds, not minutes, once the run is under way.

The startup witness recomputes the digest, the file count, the no-RECORD-reference count, the
standard-library count, the uncovered-`sys.path` list, both identity versions and `sys.version`
before request 1 of every session, and names each RECORD hash mismatch and each missing RECORD file
as its own row.

**The executor sanitizes what the cells run under** (C1(a)). Every cell used to inherit
`os.environ` whole. In confirmatory mode `run_arms.sanitized_cell_environment()` strips
`PYTHONPATH`, `PYTHONHOME` and `PYTHONSTARTUP` from the subprocess environment and sets
`PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX` to the session's fresh cache directory, and the executor journals what it did
as `cell_environment_sealed` — fail-closed, before the first cell, because a sanitization that was
performed and not recorded reads afterwards exactly like one that never happened. A pilot schedule
is left alone and says so in its record. Stripping protects the CELLS; the survey and the witness
above are what catch an injection in the EXECUTOR, which is the process that would otherwise strip
the evidence of its own contamination.

#### 3.1b The instrument is verified PER CELL and PER REQUEST, and drift is refused (Codex T51 §2)

The startup witness authenticates the tree before the session. It does not FREEZE it. The schedule
lock serialises executors; it does not prevent a file edit, and every cell is a new subprocess, so
a file changed after startup affects every later cell. Codex Turn 51 §2's concrete bad execution:
pass startup, change an executable file before a later cell, let that fresh subprocess write a row
bearing the changed digest, and render the table — which reported "DIFFERENT from the sealed
instrument tree" and computed the confirmatory estimates anyway.

**The verification schedule**, all of it inside the cell subprocess that actually spends the call:

| when | what | measured cost |
|---|---|---|
| before request 1 of the cell | execution tree **and** runtime environment | ≈79 ms + 2–20 s |
| immediately before **every** provider request, after the pacing sleep | execution tree | ≈79 ms |
| after the last write, before the cell may be complete | execution tree **and** runtime environment | ≈79 ms + 2–20 s |

The **capability probe** is a provider call the EXECUTOR makes rather than a cell subprocess, so
`run_arms.py` arms itself with the same sealed digests the moment its startup witness goes green:
the probe's requests sit behind the same per-request tree check as every cell's, instead of resting
on a witness that was green a minute earlier.

His closure 3 asks for both digests before every provider call, "if the cost allows". It does not:
an environment walk per REQUEST is ≈2 s at the very best and 15–20 s in ordinary conditions — 50 s
to 8 minutes per 25-turn rollout, and DAYS over a 144-cell panel. Two walks per CELL is 10 minutes
to 1.2 hours over the whole panel, against a 6–7 hour experiment. So the environment is verified
per CELL and the tree per REQUEST. **The residual, stated
narrowly:** a site-packages byte edit landing between one cell's opening and closing environment
checks can affect the requests of THAT ONE CELL. It cannot escape detection — the closing check
refuses the cell, its row is withdrawn and the executor stops the session — and it cannot reach any
later cell, whose own opening check runs first. Repository content has no such window at all.

**On a mismatch:** no provider call is made (the check raises a `BaseException` after the pacing
sleep and before the request function is reached, so no framework `except Exception` can turn it
into a logged attempt), no row is written (anything this process had already written for the cell
is withdrawn; bytes that existed before it are preserved), the process exits
`measure_budget.INSTRUMENT_DRIFT_EXIT` (6), and `run_arms.py` journals `execution_integrity /
instrument_drift` **fail-closed** and **stops the session** — a drifted instrument invalidates
everything after it, so nothing later could be attributed to the sealed one either.

**Hard admission, not a warning.** `instrument_identity_version`, `execution_tree_digest` and
`runtime_environment_digest` are part of `schedule_arms.contract_expectations()`, i.e. of EXACT row
identity (§3.2). A row whose digests differ from the seal, or that carries none at all, is not that
cell's row: it is an `execution_integrity` quarantine, it enters no estimand, and `arm_table`
**exits 4** naming it. The same exit 4 covers an `instrument_drift` event in the execution journal.

#### 3.1c The residual perimeter — ACCEPTED AS FINAL

Three closures above (C1, C2, C3) each removed a specific, demonstrated way to change what the
interpreter executes without moving the digest. What is left is stated here once, deliberately, and
is **not** on the backlog: it is the accepted boundary of this instrument.

**(i) The checkers verify themselves, in-process.** `execution_tree_digest()`,
`runtime_environment_manifest()` and the startup witness all live inside the very tree and the very
environment they authenticate, and they run in the same process. A mutated checker — a
`schedule_arms.py` edited to return the sealed constant, or a `_digest_file` that lies — passes its
own witness perfectly. No amount of further hashing fixes this: a self-check cannot outrank the
code performing it. The only real closure is EXTERNAL: an immutable image identified by digest, a
read-only mount, or a content-addressed environment artefact that something outside the run
verifies. **None of those exists on this machine — confirmed, not assumed:** no container, no image
digest, no read-only mount, no ACL on `.venv` or on the interpreter, no reproducible environment
artefact (this is Codex T51's Q1, answered honestly rather than closed). We are not going to build
one, and no further perimeter work is planned: no container, no signing, no external store.

**(ii) `.pyc` is excluded, and made sound rather than closed.** The exclusion cannot be removed —
bytecode is written by importing, and this venv is shared — so the closure is the fresh cache prefix
of C2: no pre-existing `__pycache__` is ever on the path, so stale or tampered bytecode is not
reachable, and every skipped `.pyc` was compiled this session from `.py` bytes this manifest
hashed. One seam remains inside this: the executor sets its own `sys.pycache_prefix` at import,
which covers everything it imports afterwards including the package, but a `.pyc` for `run_arms`
itself was already consulted by the time the redirect runs. That collapses into (i) — a tampered
`run_arms` bytecode IS a mutated checker — and every CELL, which is where every provider call is
spent, is covered from process start by the inherited environment variable.

**(iii) The threat model, stated so nobody has to guess it.** This is a measurement run by the
operator, on the operator's own machine, with no adversary present and no external immutability
control available. The byte seal is **tamper-EVIDENCE and reproducibility provenance**, not a
defence against a privileged local attacker: it exists so that an accidental `pip install`, a
half-finished edit, a stale worktree, a shadowing module or a `PYTHONPATH` left over from another
task cannot silently change what produced a row, and so that a reader months later can name exactly
which bytes ran. Against someone with write access to the checkout, the venv and this document, it
does not hold and is not claimed to. That is the accepted threat model, and it is why the closures
stop here.

The schedule is sealed on the checkout that will execute it, with the execution paths clean, by:

```
.venv/Scripts/python tests/schedule_arms.py --seal --label confirm1v4 --provider mistral \
    --models devstral-2512 ministral-14b-2512 ministral-8b-2512 mistral-medium-2508 \
    --selectors train:1 train:12 train:30 eval:5 train:3:hard train:107:hard \
    --arms A B1 B2 --replicates 2 --timeout 600
```

which prints the new `schedule_id`, the execution paths and exclusions, the on-disk execution-tree
digest with its file count, and every other sealed field. It refuses a dirty EXECUTION path (and
reports, without refusing, a dirty evidence file), refuses an EMPTY execution set, refuses to
replace an existing sealed schedule, and refuses to seal at all if the serving door cannot name the
public task id of every selector. Committing the resulting schedule file
afterwards is now legal by construction: it changes no execution path.

> **Seal under the EVALUATOR's own key**, with no `PIV_EVAL_SECRET` in the environment. The
> selector → public-task-id map and the manifest rotation/content digest are both properties of
> the active evaluator secret: sealed under a development secret they name development worlds and
> a null rotation, and the run would then be registered against worlds it will not serve. (The
> startup witness would still pass, because it resolves the secret the same way the sealing did —
> which is exactly why the operator, not the instrument, has to get this one right.)

**The startup witness** (`tests/startup_witness.py`) recomputes every one of them from the live
checkout, the installed libraries, the package and the active manifest **before the first provider
call of every session**, including every resumed one, and refuses to start when any differs,
naming the field. `run_arms --dry-run` runs the identical witness and prints it. This is the
executable form of the pinned-worktree promise the pilot broke.

### 3.2 Exact cell identity (Codex T49 §3)

Ordinals are **replicate-major over the fixed roster**, so a replicate-1 cell's planned ordinal,
block, permutation and arm position do not depend on how many replicates were requested — the
staged-`--replicate` defect of the previous design cannot recur.

A confirmatory cell counts as EXECUTED only when its own output file contains **exactly one** row,
and that row matches **all** of

    schedule_id, tag, provider, model, selector, replicate, arm,
    planned_ordinal, block_id, permutation_index, arm_position

and carries the sealed contract's `task_id`, `episode_contract_digest`,
`replay_contract_digest`, per-turn cap and library versions. Anything else — a missing
`schedule_id`, a partial identity, a duplicate, a foreign row, an unparseable file — is an
**`execution_integrity` quarantine**: named and listed, counted as neither run nor unrun, entering
no estimate, and **never re-run over** (re-running would overwrite an observed result). The old
"`schedule_id is None` is compatible" and "tag OR partial identity" paths remain for pilot
schedules and are unreachable for a sealed one.

`tests/arm_table.py` loads the **exact 144 expected paths derived from the schedule**, never a tag
substring glob, refuses duplicate rows for one cell, and refuses any file carrying this schedule's
label that is not one of those paths. Every denominator is computed from that canonical cell map.

### 3.3 Immutability (Codex T49 §4)

- Row files are written atomically (temp file + `os.replace`), so a reader never sees a partial
  one — existence alone once let a process killed mid-write leave truncated JSON that the executor
  skipped forever and the table dropped with a warning.
- **`--force` is refused outright** for a sealed schedule, in `run_arms` and in `schedule_arms`
  (which will not replace a sealed schedule file at all). Re-running a cell after seeing its
  outcome is outcome-dependent replacement of a bad draw. An instrument defect is repaired by a
  NEW schedule, or by a predeclared replacement record that preserves the original row and its
  reason.
- **There is no operator toggle for completion.** `--schedule-complete` is refused for a sealed
  schedule; run closure is DERIVED from the exact cell map (every cell has exactly one exact row
  and no integrity quarantine remains). An incomplete panel is reported incomplete.
- **The WRITER refuses the overwrite, not only the executor.** `measure_budget.py` refuses to
  write a `budget_*.json` that already exists when either the existing rows or the new run carry a
  `schedule_id`, and **no flag overrides it**. The executor's `--force` refusal is not enough on
  its own: a hand-typed `measure_budget.py --tag confirm1v4_B1p_train1_r1 --stamp-date ...` writes
  the same filename directly, and the write is atomic, so nothing afterwards would show that an
  observed cell had been replaced by a fresh draw. A plain pilot overwrite (neither side
  scheduled) is unaffected.
- `tests/stamp_contract_digest.py` refuses to edit any archived file containing a row with a
  `schedule_id`. For a row belonging to a **sealed** schedule — or to a schedule id whose file
  cannot be located, since "I could not check" is not "it is safe" — the refusal is absolute:
  `--allow-scheduled-rows` covers only a pilot schedule's rows.

### 3.4 One executor, whole blocks (Codex T49 §5)

- A single **schedule-level lock**, `<schedule>.lock`, taken `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` at executor start
  and carrying session id, **nonce**, pid, host and start time. **No automatic stale takeover**: a
  stale lock is reported with the instruction to verify the holder is dead, and `--take-over-lock`
  is an explicit operator act that is written into the arms log. Two executors invalidate the
  planned temporal order even when they never duplicate a cell, and Williams order is an execution
  property, not a JSON property.
- **The takeover is itself an ATOMIC COMPETITION** (Codex T51 §3). The retired implementation wrote
  the lock body with `path.write_text(...)` — no exclusion at all — so two recovery operators could
  observe the same stale lock, both overwrite it, both return as owners and then execute different
  cells concurrently. `--take-over-lock` is intended for a single manually coordinated operator
  (his Q3), but the safety claim may not depend on human coordination, so the exclusivity is now
  encoded:
    1. **age.** A lock younger than `TAKEOVER_MIN_LOCK_AGE_SECONDS` (300 s) is a live executor, not
       a corpse; the flag's contract is "I have verified that process is dead" and a lock created
       moments ago cannot have been verified dead. This also stops a late contender from displacing
       the brand-new lock the winner of the same race has just written;
    2. **the guard.** A separate `<schedule>.lock.takeover` file, `O_CREAT | O_EXCL`. Exactly one
       contender gets it; the rest are told a takeover is in progress and refuse. It is released in
       a `finally`, so a crashed takeover does not wedge the next one out of existence;
    3. **revalidate under the guard.** The lock must still be BYTE-FOR-BYTE the one this process
       judged stale. A contender that arrives after the winner replaced it sees different bytes —
       or no lock at all — and refuses: the corpse it was authorised to take over is not the lock
       now present;
    4. **archive, then remove, as one atomic rename.** The displaced bytes go to
       `<schedule>.lock.displaced.<session>.json` and the lock is gone in the same `os.replace`, so
       there is no instant in which the bytes are archived but the lock still stands. The rename is
       retried briefly: on Windows a rival contender reading the very same lock holds it open and
       the rename answers `WinError 32` until it lets go (observed directly in the four-thread
       witness);
    5. **acquire through the same `O_EXCL` path a clean startup uses**, then **re-read the lock and
       prove its nonce is ours** before anything executes. The clean path proves ownership too.
  The takeover is journalled fail-closed with the displaced session, the archive file name and the
  new nonce, so it is reconstructable rather than merely asserted. A four-contender witness
  requires **exactly one** to proceed.
- The per-cell `<output>.claim` stays as a second belt, `O_EXCL` as before, but is no longer taken
  over automatically either, and **release verifies ownership** — the previous release unlinked
  whatever claim it found, so a late old owner could delete a new owner's claim.
- **An unreadable lock or claim file is held by an UNKNOWN session.** A file that exists is a
  claim by someone; failing to parse it is a reason to refuse, not a licence. It is never
  unlinked by a release (a release without a session id refuses outright), acquiring names it as
  UNREADABLE, and only `--take-over-lock` clears it.
- **The window ledger fails LOUD** (§6): an append that cannot be written raises, the failure is
  stamped on the attempt as `ledger_write_failed`, and the row re-derives as
  `budget_accounting_suspicious = window_ledger_gap` — suspicious, not invalid, because a
  bookkeeping failure does not touch the token accounting. A ledger lock that cannot be taken
  **refuses the request before it is sent**: one executor runs a schedule, so contention is a
  fault, not a case to survive, and a request made without pacing evidence cannot be classified
  afterwards.
- **Malformed ledger evidence makes the ledger UNHEALTHY, and an unhealthy ledger refuses the next
  provider request** (Codex T50 §5). The retired reader skipped every JSON parse failure in
  silence. A killed process leaves a truncated final line; the next append concatenates onto it,
  so the damaged record becomes a malformed MIDDLE line and takes the following record with it —
  and the reader then undercounts the window, paces from an older request, attaches no suspicion
  and continues as though the evidence were complete. **The recovery protocol** is:
    1. any malformed or non-dict line, and any file that ends mid-record, makes the ledger
       unhealthy. `window_ledger_read` raises, `window_ledger_precheck` refuses before the request
       is sent, and `window_ledger_append` refuses rather than concatenating onto the damage —
       **scanning INSIDE its own append lock**, because outside it the check was a TOCTOU window
       and a writer that truncated the file between the scan and the lock got its damage appended
       onto, merging two records into one malformed line;
    2. **the bytes are preserved.** Nothing is repaired, rewritten or deleted. The single write
       recovery makes to existing content is a terminating newline when the file ends mid-record,
       without which the next append would destroy the following record too; the boundary record
       says it did this (`terminated_partial_line`);
    3. **recovery is an explicit operator act** — `tests/run_arms.py --recover-window-ledger`,
       refused when the ledger is healthy — which appends a `window_ledger_recovery` segment
       boundary naming the damaged line numbers and acknowledging them, and is JOURNALLED
       fail-closed as `window_ledger_recovered`. **It runs only after the startup witness is
       green**: it is the one mutating operation a sealed schedule permits, and it must not be
       made from a checkout the witness is about to refuse. The ledger-health row is skipped for
       that pass — its failure is the reason recovery was asked for — and re-checked immediately
       after the boundary lands;
    4. every window that **spans** the boundary is `evidence_incomplete` by construction, so every
       rate-limit classification inside the recovered segment is
       `ambiguous / rate_limit_evidence_incomplete`. A NEW malformed line after a recovery makes
       the ledger unhealthy again: the boundary acknowledges the past, never the future.
- **The execution journal fails CLOSED in confirmatory mode** (Codex T50 §6). The retired append
  was `except OSError: pass`, while this document claimed that a takeover is journalled BEFORE the
  probe, that a crashed cell stays visible through `cell_started`, that the actual order can be
  reconstructed and that capability exclusions and split sessions are recorded — every one of
  those claims conditional on nothing having gone wrong. The append is now taken under the same
  exclusive lock as the window ledger, flushed and fsync'd, and its success is CHECKED: in
  confirmatory mode a failure raises and **aborts the action the entry authorizes**, and
  `run_arms.py` exits 5. Every entry carries the runtime HEAD, the execution-tree digest and the
  runtime-environment digest. The startup witness runs a **create / append / read-back probe on the
  real journal file before request 1**. A pilot schedule keeps the lenient path for an unwritable
  path, and the table labels it as a pilot.
- **... and fail-closed on CORRUPTION, in every mode** (Codex T51 §4). Turn 50 closed the WRITE
  side and left the CONTENT side open: the append did not validate the existing records, and the
  probe appended a token and checked only that its OWN token came back — which an
  already-truncated line does not disturb. So a crash during an append left a malformed TAIL, the
  next startup appended a successful probe after it, and the malformed tail became a malformed
  MIDDLE, taking the following record with it. The audit events that explain takeover, recovery,
  inconclusive classification and integrity state then stopped being a complete machine-readable
  sequence while the confirmatory table still rendered. The protocol is now the window ledger's,
  exactly:
    1. **the WHOLE file is parsed under the same append lock, before every append and before the
       probe.** Any malformed or non-object line, and any file that ends mid-record, makes the
       journal unhealthy: nothing is appended and the action the entry authorizes is aborted. This
       holds in the pilot's lenient mode too — an unwritable path is a condition a pilot may shrug
       off, damaged evidence is not;
    2. **the bytes are preserved.** Nothing is repaired, rewritten or deleted;
    3. **the recovery policy is Codex's own Q4 answer.** BEFORE the first real row exists there is
       **no recovery path**: nothing has been observed, so `--recover-execution-journal` refuses and
       says ABORT AND RESEAL — cut a new label and leave these bytes as evidence. AFTER at least
       one cell has an exactly-matching row, recovery is the same explicit operator act the ledger
       uses: `tests/run_arms.py --recover-execution-journal` appends an immutable
       `execution_journal_recovery` **segment boundary** that acknowledges the damaged line numbers,
       terminates a partial final line (without which the next append would destroy the following
       record too), and carries a **provenance record** — segment number, malformed lines, reason,
       session, the operator act, and the runtime identity that performed it. It runs only after
       the startup witness is green, with the journal-probe row skipped for that pass;
    4. **the table refuses over it.** `arm_table` exits 4 and refuses the confirmatory estimands
       while the journal carries a malformed line no recovery acknowledges. A recovered segment
       boundary with its provenance is **clean with a note**: the table renders the boundary and
       computes normally. A new malformed line after a recovery makes the journal unhealthy again —
       the boundary acknowledges the past, never the future.
- **`--limit` operates on whole three-arm blocks only.** A block split across sessions is not the
  block the Williams order registered; when a block is nevertheless split (an interruption), the
  executor says so and the table flags it.
- Every cell's start, finish, session id and actual ordinal are recorded on the row and in an
  append-only execution journal (`reviews/arms_<label>_execution.jsonl`), so a cell whose
  subprocess crashed without writing a row is still visible to the order census.
- `tests/arm_table.py` prints **both** censuses: the scheduled sequence/position/adjacency census
  AND the ACTUAL temporal one, reconstructed from timestamps and session ids, with any block that
  ran split or out of order named. A block containing a cell with **no execution timestamp** is
  marked UNORDERED rather than sorted into an invented order: its executed sequence is unknown,
  which is not the same as matching the plan.
